body:
Why hazard symbols are used

Chemicals can present different types of danger. Some ignite easily, some injure the skin or eyes, some cause serious poisoning, and others can harm aquatic life. A label must communicate the relevant danger clearly, even before the user has detailed knowledge of the chemical.

The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) provides an international approach to classifying chemical hazards and communicating them through labels and safety information. Its familiar pictograms have a symbol within a diamond-shaped red border.

The 9 main GHS pictograms

The pictograms indicate types of hazards, not the concentration of a chemical or a universal numerical danger score.

  • Exploding bomb: Warns of explosive hazards or certain substances capable of dangerous self-reactive behaviour.
  • Flame: Indicates flammable materials or other specified fire-related hazards.
  • Flame over circle: Indicates an oxidising hazard. An oxidiser can intensify a fire even when it is not itself a combustible fuel.
  • Gas cylinder: Indicates gases stored under pressure.
  • Corrosion: Warns of severe skin burns, serious eye damage or corrosive effects on metals, according to the chemical's classification.
  • Skull and crossbones: Indicates severe acute toxicity, including hazards that can cause fatal or toxic effects after relatively short exposure.
  • Exclamation mark: Commonly indicates irritation, harmful acute toxicity or certain sensitising effects.
  • Human silhouette with a mark on the chest: Indicates important health hazards such as carcinogenicity, respiratory sensitisation or certain forms of organ toxicity.
  • Dead tree and fish: Indicates environmental hazards, particularly toxicity to aquatic organisms.

Important distinctions between similar symbols

Flame versus flame over circle

The flame symbol commonly warns that a substance may catch fire. The flame-over-circle symbol warns that a substance may intensify combustion by acting as an oxidiser. These are different properties.

Exclamation mark versus skull and crossbones

The exclamation mark can indicate harmful effects such as skin irritation or a less severe category of acute toxicity. The skull and crossbones is associated with more severe acute toxicity classifications. The precise meaning depends on the classification and label statements.

Corrosion versus general irritation

The corrosion symbol may indicate serious burns or eye damage. The exclamation mark may indicate less severe irritation. A chemical's full label must be read because pictograms do not communicate every relevant detail.

Other information on chemical labels

Hazard communication also uses a product identifier, hazard statements, precautionary statements and, where applicable, a signal word. The signal words Danger and Warning communicate different levels of severity within the applicable hazard classifications; Danger is used for more severe categories.

A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) provides more detailed information about a chemical, including its hazards, safe handling, storage and emergency precautions. Pictograms provide rapid recognition but do not replace the full label or safety information.

GHS provides an international system, but the precise pictograms required on labels depend on the regulations adopted in a particular jurisdiction. The environmental pictogram is part of the GHS set even though it is not mandatory under the United States OSHA workplace-label system.

Prelims focus

  • GHS stands for Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals.
  • There are 9 commonly recognised GHS hazard pictograms.
  • Flame over circle indicates an oxidising hazard.
  • Gas cylinder indicates gas under pressure.
  • Skull and crossbones indicates severe acute toxicity.
  • Trap: The dead-tree-and-fish symbol concerns environmental hazard, not the same hazard as the human-health silhouette.

[Sources: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals, 11th revised edition, published September 2025, introduction and hazard communication provisions; UNECE, GHS Pictograms, consulted 3 November 2026; United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Hazard Communication Standard Pictogram Quick Card, OSHA 3491-08R, 2024; OSHA, Hazard Communication Standard, Appendix C, Allocation of Label Elements, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: All 9 GHS red-diamond pictograms, with flame beside oxidiser and exclamation mark beside skull and crossbones for comparison.
pictures.caption: The 9 GHS pictograms identify different physical, health and environmental hazards.

title: Chemical Hazard Symbols: Recognising the GHS Pictograms

body:
Safety begins before a chemical is used

A chemical may be useful when handled correctly and dangerous when used carelessly. Household cleaners, pesticides, paints, solvents and other products should therefore be handled according to their labels and the hazards they present.

Safe handling does not mean treating every substance identically. A flammable solvent, a corrosive cleaner and a pressurised gas container require different precautions. Their labels identify the relevant hazards and recommended measures.

Basic safe-handling principles

  1. Identify the chemical. Read its name, hazard symbols and instructions before use. Do not use an unidentified substance.
  2. Use only as directed. Follow the stated purpose and precautions. Do not assume that a larger quantity is safer or more effective.
  3. Prevent exposure. Avoid unnecessary breathing of vapours, skin contact and splashes. Use suitable ventilation and recommended gloves or eye protection when required.
  4. Avoid incompatible mixtures. Do not combine chemicals or cleaning products unless their instructions explicitly permit it.
  5. Maintain hygiene. Avoid eating or drinking while handling hazardous chemicals and wash hands after use.
  6. Manage leftovers and waste safely. Follow product and local waste-disposal instructions rather than pouring hazardous residues into drains or onto soil.

Storage and labelling

Chemicals should generally remain in their original labelled containers, properly closed and stored as directed. They must be kept away from food and drinking water and out of the reach of children and pets. Flammable substances should be kept away from ignition sources according to their labels.

Transferring a chemical into an empty drinking-water or soft-drink bottle creates a serious risk of accidental swallowing. A person may mistake the contents for something safe to drink, especially when the original warning label has been removed.

Why household chemicals must not be mixed

Some familiar products react dangerously when combined. Bleach should not be mixed with other cleaning products. In particular, mixing bleach with ammonia-containing products or acidic cleaners can release dangerous gases that may seriously injure the respiratory system.

Using separate products is not automatically safe if one remains on the surface when another is applied. Cleaning and disinfecting should follow the manufacturer's directions, including precautions about ventilation and incompatible chemicals.

Never use smell, colour or familiarity as proof that a chemical is safe. Some dangerous substances have little noticeable odour, and a household product can still be corrosive, toxic or irritating.

What to do after an accidental exposure

If a chemical spill or exposure occurs, the first priority is to prevent further contact without placing another person in danger. Leave an area containing hazardous fumes, warn others and obtain suitable assistance. For skin or eye exposure, follow the product's first-aid instructions; these commonly include prompt rinsing with clean running water. Seek medical advice or emergency help when the exposure is serious or symptoms occur.

Do not attempt to neutralise a chemical on the skin by applying another chemical. Such reactions may cause additional injury. For a significant spill, unknown substance or suspected toxic gas release, use trained emergency assistance rather than attempting an improvised cleanup.

Safe disposal protects the environment

Paints, solvents, pesticides, motor oil and similar materials should not be emptied into drains or onto open land. They can contaminate water and soil or interfere with organisms involved in wastewater treatment. Hazardous waste requires appropriate collection and disposal arrangements.

Prelims focus

  • Read the label and identify the hazard before handling a chemical.
  • Keep chemicals in properly labelled containers and away from food and children.
  • Bleach must not be mixed with ammonia-containing products or acidic cleaners.
  • Ventilation and suitable protective equipment reduce exposure.
  • Hazardous chemical waste should not be poured into drains or onto soil.
  • Trap: A stronger mixture or a larger quantity does not automatically make a cleaning product safer.

[Sources: CDC, Cleaning and Disinfecting with Bleach, dated 24 April 2024, sections on safe use, ventilation and mixing precautions; CDC, How to Safely Clean and Sanitize with Bleach, dated 26 August 2026, section Follow Safety Instructions; CDC, Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, Chlorine, ToxFAQs, section on reducing household exposure, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 18, Wastewater Story, section 18.5, Better Housekeeping Practices, 2018–19 edition; OSHA, Hazard Communication Standard, Appendix C, Precautionary Statements, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Safe chemical use requires precautions before, during and after handling.

title: Safe Chemical Handling, Storage and Emergency Precautions

body:
Preventing pollution at its source

Environmental protection is most effective when unnecessary pollution is prevented before it enters air, water or soil. Once pollutants spread, they may be difficult to remove and may affect locations far from their source.

The appropriate control depends on the pollutant and the medium affected. Reducing fuel combustion helps limit some air pollutants. Preventing untreated sewage discharge protects water bodies. Correct handling of pesticides and industrial waste reduces the risk of soil and groundwater contamination.

Basic methods of pollution prevention

Pollution problemPreventive approachMain benefit
Vehicle and fuel emissionsCleaner transport, suitable fuels and vehicle maintenanceReduced harmful air emissions
Domestic sewageSanitation and wastewater treatmentLower microbial and organic pollution of water
Industrial wastewaterAppropriate treatment before dischargeReduced chemical contamination of water
Open dumping and burningWaste segregation, collection and safe disposalLess soil contamination and smoke
Excess agricultural chemicalsCareful input use and prevention of runoffReduced nutrient and pesticide pollution

Important Indian environmental laws

India has enacted legislation addressing pollution prevention and environmental protection. At the prelims level, the following law-year associations are important:

  • Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974: Provides a framework for preventing and controlling water pollution and for pollution-control institutions.
  • Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981: Addresses prevention, control and abatement of air pollution.
  • Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: Provides a broader framework for measures to protect and improve environmental quality.

Central and Gujarat pollution-control institutions

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) operates at the national level and undertakes functions relating to pollution prevention, monitoring and technical coordination under applicable environmental laws.

In Gujarat, the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) is the state pollution-control institution. The Government of Gujarat constituted GPCB on 15 October 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. Its work concerns pollution prevention and control, including functions relating to water and air quality.

Selected national programmes

National Clean Air Programme

The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) was launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January 2019. It seeks to improve urban air quality through coordinated measures, monitoring and city-specific action plans.

A Ministry statement dated 8 August 2024 identified Ahmedabad, Rajkot, Surat and Vadodara as the 4 Gujarat cities covered in its reported programme assessment. For the data period 2023–24, it reported reductions in annual PM10 concentrations compared with the 2017–18 baseline. These are historical findings from that dated statement, not claims about measurements or programme coverage in November 2026.

Swachh Bharat Mission

The Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014 to improve sanitation and cleanliness. Its rural component addresses safe sanitation, prevention of open defecation and management of solid and liquid waste. Better sanitation reduces the possibility that untreated human waste will contaminate soil and drinking-water sources.

Namami Gange Programme

The Namami Gange Programme was launched in June 2014 for pollution abatement, conservation and rejuvenation of the River Ganga and its tributaries. Its activities have included sewage-treatment infrastructure, river cleaning, awareness and industrial-effluent monitoring. Its launch and objectives are historical facts; the programme's administrative duration and project status may change.

Connecting a pollutant to the correct response

Different pollution problems require different responses. Carbon monoxide exposure is addressed by preventing unsafe combustion and inhalation, not by boiling drinking water. Excess nitrates and phosphates entering a pond require attention to nutrient inputs and wastewater, not only removal of visible floating debris. Soil contamination requires preventing chemical releases, while protection from soil erosion also depends on conserving vegetation and topsoil.

Prelims focus

  • Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act: 1974.
  • Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act: 1981.
  • Environment (Protection) Act: 1986.
  • Gujarat Pollution Control Board was constituted on 15 October 1974.
  • National Clean Air Programme was launched in January 2019.
  • Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014; Namami Gange was launched in June 2014.
  • Trap: A dated report about air-quality improvements does not establish the measured air quality of those cities in a later year.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, introduction and sections 16.1–16.3; Gujarat Pollution Control Board, About Us, official GPCB information service, consulted 3 November 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Goals Set under NCAP, released 8 August 2024, including Gujarat city coverage and data for 2017–18 and 2023–24; Ministry of Jal Shakti, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin), About Us, consulted 3 November 2026; National Mission for Clean Ganga, Namami Gange Programme, programme overview, consulted 3 November 2026.]
